citation: Rames MM, Rios-Duarte JA, Vidal NY. The Safety of Perioperative Liposomal Bupivacaine Injections in Dermatologic Surgery Patients. Dermatol Surg 2026;52(8):743-747
text_quality: ok (5 PDF pages, complete: abstract, introduction, methods, results, Table 1 over PDF pp. 3-4, discussion, limitations, references 1-23). Extraction oddities: '=' appears as '5' ('n 5 85'), '≥' as '$', '<' as ',', '>' as '.', '±' as '6', '+' as '1'. The paper's own counts are internally inconsistent: the abstract gives 140 administrations in 129 patients (excisions 88, Mohs 49, hidradenitis 77) and 'no adverse events in 134 out of 136 patients', while the Results and Table 1 give 136 administrations in 127 patients (excisions 85, Mohs 48, hidradenitis 74); repair-type counts also differ between text and Table 1.
design: Retrospective single-institution chart review (descriptive case series, no comparator group). Electronic health records searched for 'Exparel' and 'liposomal bupivacaine'; adverse events taken from chart documentation; absence of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) inferred from lack of documentation.
population: Adults (18 years or older) who received perioperative liposomal bupivacaine at the surgical site during dermatologic surgery, October 2015 to October 2024; 52% male, median age 48.6 years. Most frequent diagnoses: hidradenitis suppurativa (54.4%) and cutaneous neoplasms (41.2%, most often squamous cell carcinoma); most frequent sites: axillae, groin, anogenital region, face, scalp and neck. Ten patients were on opioids at baseline. No neuropathy population.
n: 136 administrations in 127 patients per Results and Table 1 (abstract: 140 administrations, 129 patients); single arm. Procedures: excision 85 (62.5%), Mohs micrographic surgery 48 (35.3%), Mohs with nail avulsion 2, other 1.
setting: Mayo Clinic, Rochester, Minnesota (Department of Dermatology / Division of Dermatologic Surgery); outpatient dermatologic surgery, plus operating-room cases (e.g. hidradenitis) done under sedation or anaesthesia.
intervention: Liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel), [dose figure omitted], given once per procedure by local infiltration at the surgical site and surrounding skin after the procedure was complete (three patients had a repeat administration within a short interval; the table footnote says their totals stayed under the labelled limit). Initial local anaesthesia was lidocaine or buffered lidocaine; liposomal bupivacaine was injected separately afterwards, after the waiting interval the manufacturer recommends, not mixed with another local anaesthetic in the syringe. The only tissue plane the paper names is subcutaneous (for linear closures and flaps). For large hidradenitis fields the authors describe dilution with normal saline and infiltration over the wound area by a fanning technique (ratios and volumes not copied). The paper states that no case exceeded the labelled maximum for local infiltration. Nerve blocks at the institution were done with lidocaine plus plain bupivacaine or plain bupivacaine, not with liposomal bupivacaine.
comparator: None. The methods mention a Wilcoxon comparison of case characteristics between patients with and without reported postoperative pain, but no result of it is reported.
route: Local infiltration of the surgical site and surrounding skin; the only plane named is subcutaneous tissue around the flap base, pedicle and inset margins. The words 'intradermal' and 'dermal' do not occur in the paper; no nerve block with liposomal bupivacaine.
duration: Single perioperative administration; adverse events as documented in the chart. Patients were observed briefly after injection, heart rate was measured before and after, and patients were discharged with instructions to watch for signs of toxicity over the following days.
outcomes: Treatment characteristics (procedure, diagnosis, anatomical site, repair type, total wound area and length, number of operative sites, volume given) and documented adverse events, including CNS and cardiovascular signs of LAST. No pain scores, duration of anaesthesia, plasma levels or efficacy outcome were reported.

key_results.quote: A retrospective chart review was performed at a single institution using an institutional database and key words “Exparel” or “liposomal bupivacaine.”
Patients $18 years old who received perioperative LB to the surgical site and surrounding skin were included.
A total of 136 occurrences of liposomal bupivacaine [dose figure omitted] administration in 127 patients were included in the study.
There were no adverse events in 134 out of 136 cases of LB administration (98.5%). There were 2 reports (1.5%) of nausea on Postoperative day 1 (POD1) while these patients were taking opioids
Importantly, there were no CNS or CVS AEs in this cohort.
The authors observed no cases of LAST.
Liposomal bupivacaine was used most often in the setting of excisions (n 5 85, 62.5%) followed by MMS (n 5 48, 35.3%).
Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) was the most frequent diagnosis (n 5 74, 54.4%) associated with the procedure where LB was administered, followed by cutaneous neoplasms (n 5 56, 41.2%)
Injections were performed as local infiltrations.
This is injected in subcutaneous tissue around the flap base, pedicle, and inset margins.
For initial local anesthesia at this institution, lidocaine or buffered lidocaine is used, with LB reserved for after completion of complex or extensive procedures.
For cases performed in the operative room (e.g., HS cases), LB was injected immediately after the case with the patient under sedation or anesthesia.
At this institution, nerve blocks are performed per surgeon discretion, either with lidocaine mixed with plain bupivacaine or with plain bupivacaine.
Notably, LAST has not been reported in a dermatologic setting.
The specific pharmacokinetics and rates of adverse events have not been studied in dermatologic surgery
Updated labeling including indications for adductor canal block and sciatic nerve block in the popliteal fossa; 2023.

author_limitations.quote: Limitations of this study include its retrospective nature, small sample size, and single institution data.
Owing to the retrospective nature of this study, adverse events were identified through chart review, and the absence of reported LAST cases was inferred from lack of documentation.
Future prospective studies are necessary to investigate the rate of adverse events across various dermatologic procedures.
In addition, studies with a control arm are needed to evaluate the efficacy of LB versus placebo while accounting for prescription oral analgesics.

funding_conflicts: No funding source stated. Conflicts: "The authors have indicated no significant interest with commercial supporters." (PDF p. 1).

Dose safety and pharmacodynamics of subcutaneous bupivacaine in a novel extended-release microparticle formulation: a phase 1, dose-ascending study in male volunteers. Basic Clin Pharmacol Toxicol 2024;134:657-75 (ref 5)
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Sustained-release bupivacaine in human skin: subcutaneous PLGA microparticle formulation in volunteers gave hypoaesthesia and hypoalgesia lasting days (37 to 86 h), with frequent local reactions and one systemic-toxicity event (figures omitted). Bears on C043 and on the 'only human formulation that has ever produced days … of skin block' sentence on 'What is still unsettled' (finding F03); already described on 'Injectables ruled out but not tried'.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Label revision of 2023 adding two nerve-block indications; makes the route list on 'Injectables ruled out but not tried' (read from the 2021 label) outdated (findings F01, F02). Rames cites it for the labelled maxima (not copied).

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Marketed liposome bupivacaine given subcutaneously to 132 volunteers (abstract), onset of analgesia within minutes; in D048's records. PubMed's MeSH indexing nonetheless lists 'Injections, Intradermal' for it, against the abstract's 'subcutaneous'.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Zadrazil M, Marhofer P, Opfermann P, Schmid W, et al. Liposomal bupivacaine for peripheral nerve blockade: a randomized, controlled, crossover, triple-blinded pharmacodynamic study in volunteers. Anesthesiology 2024;141:24-31 (ref 20)
